n.story:
In the coming years, your expertise in the natural properties of wood will be augmented by precision digital tools. While the physical act of moving and stacking timber remains a human-led task, the 'guesswork' of chemical treatment is disappearing. AI sensors will now instantly identify wood species and moisture content, automatically calculating the exact chemical mix and pressure required for a perfect treat. You will move away from manual record-keeping and controller setup, as these tasks become background processes integrated into the machinery.

Your role evolves into a quality and contract specialist. With AI handling the technical precision of the treatment cycles, you will spend more time ensuring that the final products meet specific, complex contract requirements and managing the environmental safety of the facility. You become the bridge between the raw material and the digital system, using your tactile knowledge of wood to verify what the sensors might miss, while relying on AI to handle the administrative and chemical complexity of the job.

While the soul of your work remains in the tactile manipulation of grain and fiber, AI-powered computer vision now acts as your second set of eyes, instantly identifying wood species and internal defects that were previously invisible. You spend less time on the 'grunt work' of material preparation and more time on the conceptual design phase, using AI to simulate how different finishes will age or how complex geometric joints will bear weight over decades. You are no longer just a carver; you are a material strategist who uses technology to push the boundaries of what wood can achieve.

Your value will increasingly lie in your 'human touch'—the ability to interpret grain aesthetics, handle delicate tear-out prevention that sensors can't feel, and apply artistic intent to the infinite variations suggested by AI.
